doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Musical family and records in New Zealand, Voice of America
summary: His parents were guitar and banjo players with a big record collection; he followed jazz via DownBeat and Voice of America, and met Willis Conover.

bands.name: Miff Mole and his Little Molars

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Where did you get the music in New Zealand. Do they have decent record stores and so forth? Was your family musical?

My family was musical. In fact they told me that two weeks before I was born they got front row seats to a concert by Artie Shaw. And so they used to take me all kinds of places before I was born, so I was absorbing Artie Shaw at the time. And so they had a huge record collection. There was Artie Shaw and Woody — in fact my parents were just blown away when I got the job with Woody.

And so I was listening to Charlie Parker and Coleman Hawkins, Lester, and Basie and everybody, when I was just a little kid. Because there was no T.V. at the time when I was growing up, and so on rainy days before I went to kindergarten, my parents would just sit me in front of the — well my mother would sit me in front of the record player and just let me go. And I was listening to a lot of Dixieland as well, some Louis Armstrong, Jack Teagarden, and Miff Mole and his Little Molars. Remember them? So it was a really great musical upbringing. My parents were both guitar players and banjo players. And they used to have jam sessions at the house. So I would go to bed and hear all this great © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

stuff being played. But record stores — to a degree, to a degree. Probably a better selection of jazz record stores than we have now in the States, but I used to buy directly from the States. I had a subscription to “DownBeat” magazine and I’d read all these things, and I’d also get “Voice of America” on shortwave radio. And so I would hear all these great things like Art Blakey, Horace Silver, Max Roach, all these wonderful players. And the guy would say, “and this is from their latest album,” bang. So I would write off a letter to my contacts in San Francisco and I’d get a little package back. So that was nice.
A lot of people have mentioned “Voice of America” in Japan and Europe of course. That was really great.
And I did get to meet Willis Conover one time. He was the voice of “Voice of America” jazz. And I met him in Warsaw, in Poland, when we were with Woody.
